newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan stocks dip, dollar eases below 118 yen.
newsitem.headline: Japan stocks dip, dollar eases below 118 yen.

text.p: Japanese shares dipped on Tuesday in a volatile morning session swayed by rumours -- quickly denied -- of an official rescue for the sagging market and by worries over selling by foreign investors.
The dollar, meanwhile, was knocked back below 118 yen by profit-taking and concern that Japan's central bank may step into the currency markets to bolster the yen.

The 225-share Nikkei average slumped from the start of trade, undermined by fears that foreign investors would dump their Japanese shares rather than see the home-currency value of those holdings fall further as the yen weakens.
The Nikkei jumped briefly into positive territory on bargain-hunting and on talk that the Finance Ministry was poised to unveil special steps to prop up share prices.
But it slid again after an official denial, and ended the morning down 35.34 points or 0.20 percent at 17,445.00.
Persistent concern over Japan's economic outlook and worries about the health of the bad loan-laden financial sector have sliced nearly 10 percent off the Nikkei so far this year.
Government ministers again sought to cheer up the market with pledges to carry out promised structural economic reform.

"I think there will be moves to buy (stocks) if the public understands that the government is serious about various structural reforms," Economic Planning Agency Minister Taro Aso told a regular news conference.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told parliament on Monday he would carry out reforms in key areas including education, social security and the financial markets, but market pundits are keen to see proof of his resolve.

Hashimoto's other promise -- to forge ahead with a planned rise in Japan's sales tax and halt special income tax cuts this year -- did little to cheer a market which fears the higher tax burden could stall Japan's economic recovery.
Asked whether the government had any special stock market rescue steps in mind, Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said only that the government would keep working hard on macroeconomic policies.

The dollar, meanwhile, was trading at around 117.77 yen in mid-morning in Asia after soaring to a high of 118.29 yen in European trade, benefiting from strength in the U.S. economy and relatively attractive U.S. interest rates.

The greenback slipped back below 118 yen soon after Finance Minister Mitsuzuka told a news conference that the yen's weakness was overdone and that Japan would take "appropriate steps" against excessive currency swings.
"The recent weak trend of the yen is excessive," Mitsuzuka said. "We will keep sufficient watch on currency moves and will act properly against wild currency movements," he said.
This made the market cautious about the possibility that the Bank of Japan may intervene in the foreign exchange markets.

Some analysts have said, however, that Japanese authorities are unlikely to intervene to stem the yen's slide with anything more than words, given that other Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations, including the United States, seem content with the strong dollar.
On the bond market, the key March Japanese government bond futures contract ended the morning unchanged as investors awaited the results of a 20-year government bond auction later in the day.
